subtopics.title: MUnit Overview
subtopics.meta_description: An introduction to MUnit, MuleSoft's native testing framework: its project structure, and how to run test suites in Anypoint Studio and via Maven builds.
subtopics.summary: What MUnit is, how test suites are structured, and how tests run inside Studio and through the munit-maven-plugin.
subtopics.content_html:
Manually clicking through Anypoint Studio to verify a flow still works after every change doesn't scale, and it certainly doesn't belong in a CI/CD pipeline. MUnit is MuleSoft's own unit and integration testing framework, purpose-built to run Mule flows in isolation, mock external dependencies, and assert on the results — all without needing a live database, API, or message broker.

Where MUnit Fits

MUnit tests live alongside your application code in the same Mule project, under src/test/munit, as XML files that describe test suites and individual test cases using MUnit's own set of components layered on top of the standard Mule Core module. Because they're written in the same XML/DataWeave dialect as your application, there's no separate language or framework to learn beyond a handful of MUnit-specific elements.

Project Structure

my-mule-project/
  src/
    main/
      mule/
        customer-api.xml
    test/
      munit/
        customer-api-test-suite.xml

A test suite file typically starts by declaring the MUnit namespaces and a reference to the configuration/flows under test:

<mule xmlns:munit="http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit"
      xmlns:munit-tools="http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit-tools"
      xmlns="http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/core"
      xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
      xsi:schemaLocation="
        http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/core http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/core/current/mule.xsd
        http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit/current/mule-munit.xsd
        http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit-tools http://www.mulesoft.org/schema/mule/munit-tools/current/mule-munit-tools.xsd">

    <munit:config name="customer-api-test-suite.xml" />

</mule>

Running Tests

MUnit tests can be run directly inside Anypoint Studio via right-click > Run As > MUnit Test, which shows pass/fail results and coverage in a dedicated view. For automated pipelines, the munit-maven-plugin executes the same suites during the Maven build lifecycle (typically bound to the test phase), so a build fails automatically if any test fails — making MUnit a natural fit for CI/CD gates before deployment.

# pom.xml excerpt
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.mulesoft.munit.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>munit-maven-plugin</artifactId>
</plugin>

What MUnit Tests Typically Cover

  • Unit-level tests for a single flow or subflow, mocking every external connector call so the test runs instantly and deterministically.
  • Transformation tests that feed sample input into a flow and assert the DataWeave output is shaped correctly.
  • Error-path tests that force a mocked failure and verify the flow's error handler produces the expected response.
  • Integration-style tests against a real (often local/dockerized) backend when full end-to-end confidence is required, though these are less common than fully mocked unit tests.
Tip: Keep MUnit test suites mirroring your application's flow files one-to-one (e.g. customer-api.xml → customer-api-test-suite.xml) so tests are easy to locate as the project grows.

Why MUnit Matters for Production Confidence

Integration platforms sit in a uniquely risky position: a broken flow can silently corrupt data flowing between multiple business-critical systems, and by the time a manual tester notices, the damage may already be replicated downstream. A solid MUnit suite catches regressions the moment a flow, DataWeave transformation, or error handler changes, long before a deployment reaches production. Because tests run against mocked dependencies rather than live systems, they also execute in seconds rather than minutes, which keeps the feedback loop tight enough that developers actually run tests locally before committing, rather than treating testing as an afterthought bolted on right before release.

Key Points

  • MUnit is MuleSoft's native testing framework, written in the same XML/DataWeave style as Mule applications.
  • Test suites live under src/test/munit and run inside Studio or via the munit-maven-plugin.
  • Tests typically mock external systems so they run fast and deterministically, without live dependencies.
  • Integrating MUnit into Maven builds makes automated testing part of every CI/CD pipeline run.

subtopics.title: Writing MUnit Test Cases
subtopics.meta_description: Learn the behavior, execution and validation phases of an MUnit test case, and how to set up test events with munit:set-event before execution begins.
subtopics.summary: How to structure an MUnit test case using the behavior, execution, and validation phases with practical XML examples.
subtopics.content_html:
Every MUnit test case follows the same shape borrowed from classic unit testing: set up the conditions the flow expects, execute the flow, then verify the outcome. MUnit expresses this with the <munit:test> element and its three phases — behavior (mocks/setup), execution, and validation.

The Anatomy of a Test

<munit:test name="get-customer-by-id-test"
    description="Verifies the get-customer-by-id-subflow returns the expected customer payload">

    <munit:behavior>
        <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:select">
            <munit-tools:then-return>
                <munit-tools:payload value='#[[{ id: 1, name: "Jane Doe", email: "jane@example.com" }]]' />
            </munit-tools:then-return>
        </munit-tools:mock-when>
    </munit:behavior>

    <munit:execution>
        <flow-ref name="get-customer-by-id-subflow" />
    </munit:execution>

    <munit:validation>
        <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.name]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('Jane Doe')]" />
        <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.email]" is="#[MunitTools::notNullValue()]" />
    </munit:validation>
</munit:test>

Setting Up the Test Event

By default a test creates an empty Mule event. When the flow under test expects specific input, use <munit:set-event> inside the behavior block to set a payload, variables, or attributes before execution begins:

<munit:behavior>
    <munit:set-event>
        <munit:payload value='#[{"id": 1}]' mediaType="application/json" />
        <munit:variables>
            <munit:variable key="correlationId" value='#["test-123"]' />
        </munit:variables>
    </munit:set-event>
</munit:behavior>

Testing Flows vs Subflows

You can target a whole flow (including its listener-facing logic minus the actual HTTP source) or a specific subflow with <flow-ref> in the execution block. Testing subflows in isolation is usually preferable because it keeps each test focused on one unit of logic, rather than exercising an entire request/response chain end to end.

Organizing Suites with munit:config

Each test file typically has one <munit:config name="..."/> at the top, and multiple <munit:test> elements underneath it representing different scenarios for the flows in that file — a happy path, a validation failure, a downstream timeout, and so on.

<munit:test name="get-customer-not-found-test">
    <munit:behavior>
        <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:select">
            <munit-tools:then-return>
                <munit-tools:payload value="#[[]]" />
            </munit-tools:then-return>
        </munit-tools:mock-when>
    </munit:behavior>
    <munit:execution>
        <flow-ref name="get-customer-by-id-subflow" />
    </munit:execution>
    <munit:validation>
        <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[vars.httpStatus]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(404)]" />
    </munit:validation>
</munit:test>
Note: A test's description attribute is optional but strongly recommended — it appears in test reports and makes failures self-explanatory without opening the XML.

Naming and Organizing Tests

Consistent naming pays off quickly as a test suite grows. A common convention is <flow-or-subflow-name>-<scenario>-test, for example create-customer-success-test, create-customer-duplicate-email-test, and create-customer-invalid-payload-test sitting side by side in the same suite file. This makes test reports scannable at a glance and helps new team members understand exactly which behaviors are already covered before adding new logic. It is also worth keeping each test focused on a single scenario rather than chaining several unrelated assertions together, since a failure in a narrowly scoped test immediately tells you which specific behavior broke, while a sprawling test with a dozen assertions leaves you guessing until you read through the whole thing.

Key Points

  • Every MUnit test has three phases: behavior (setup/mocks), execution, and validation (assertions).
  • munit:set-event lets you control payload, variables, and attributes before the flow runs.
  • Prefer testing focused subflows over entire request/response flows for clearer, more maintainable tests.
  • Write one test per scenario (happy path, error path, edge case) rather than cramming many assertions into one test.

subtopics.title: Mocking in MUnit
subtopics.meta_description: Master MUnit mocking with mock-when, then-return, then-throw, spy-when and verify-call to isolate Mule flows from real external systems during testing.
subtopics.summary: How to isolate Mule flows from real external systems using MUnit's mock-when, spy-when, and verify-call components.
subtopics.content_html:
Real MUnit tests almost never talk to a real database, HTTP API, or message queue — doing so would make tests slow, flaky, and dependent on external systems being available. Instead, MUnit lets you mock any processor's behavior, substituting a controlled, predictable response in its place.

mock-when

The core mocking component is <munit-tools:mock-when>, placed inside a test's behavior block. It targets a processor by its namespace and operation name, optionally narrows the match using attribute conditions, and defines what should happen when that processor is invoked during the test.

<munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
    <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="#['/customers']" name="path" />
    </munit-tools:with-attributes>
    <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value='#[{ "id": 1, "name": "Jane Doe" }]' mediaType="application/json" />
        <munit-tools:attributes value="#[{statusCode: 200}]" />
    </munit-tools:then-return>
</munit-tools:mock-when>

with-attributes lets you mock a processor differently depending on how it's invoked — for example, returning a success payload for one path and a 404 for another, or matching a specific SQL query for a Database connector call. Without it, every invocation of the matched processor in that test returns the same mocked response.

Simulating Errors

To test error-handling paths, use <munit-tools:then-throw> instead of then-return to make the mocked processor raise an error:

<munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:select">
    <munit-tools:then-throw>
        <munit-tools:error-type>DB:CONNECTIVITY</munit-tools:error-type>
    </munit-tools:then-throw>
</munit-tools:mock-when>

This makes it straightforward to verify that a flow's on-error-continue or on-error-propagate blocks behave correctly without needing to actually break a real downstream connection.

spy-when

Sometimes you don't want to replace a processor's behavior, only observe it — confirming a processor was called, or inspecting the event before and after it runs. <munit-tools:spy-when> does this without altering the real outcome:

<munit-tools:spy-when processor="logger">
    <munit-tools:before-call>
        <munit-tools:set-event>
            <munit:variables>
                <munit:variable key="spyHit" value="#[true]" />
            </munit:variables>
        </munit-tools:set-event>
    </munit-tools:before-call>
</munit-tools:spy-when>

Verifying Call Counts

MUnit also provides <munit-tools:verify-call> to assert how many times a processor was invoked, which is useful for confirming retry logic or making sure an expensive operation was only called once:

<munit-tools:verify-call processor="http:request" times="1" />
Tip: Mock at the connector-operation level (e.g. db:select, http:request) rather than mocking an entire subflow, so your test still exercises all the real transformation and routing logic between the mocked boundary and the assertion.

Global Mocks Versus Per-Test Mocks

MUnit lets you declare mocks either inside an individual test's behavior block, scoping them to just that test, or inside a suite-level <munit:before-test> block that runs before every test in the file. Suite-level mocks are convenient for a dependency that behaves the same way across most scenarios, such as a configuration lookup or a logging call you never want to actually execute during tests. Test-level mocks should be preferred whenever the mocked response needs to vary by scenario, since overriding a suite-level mock inside a single test can be confusing to read later. A good rule of thumb is to keep mocking as close as possible to the test that depends on it, only promoting a mock to the suite level once you have genuinely repeated the exact same mock-when block across several tests.

Key Points

  • mock-when replaces a processor's real behavior with a controlled payload, attributes, or error.
  • with-attributes lets a single test mock the same processor differently based on how it was called.
  • then-throw simulates errors to test error-handling paths without a real failing dependency.
  • spy-when and verify-call let you observe and assert on processor invocation without changing behavior.

subtopics.title: MUnit HTTP and Database Mocking Examples
subtopics.meta_description: Worked MUnit examples showing how to mock an HTTP Request connector and a Database Select operation so tests run without any real network or database access.
subtopics.summary: Mocking HTTP and Database operations with mock-when and then-return lets MUnit tests exercise flow logic without ever touching a real network or database.
subtopics.content_html:
A flow that calls a third-party HTTP API and then persists the result to a database is exactly the kind of flow that is easy to leave untested, because testing it "for real" means depending on external systems being up, reachable, and in a known state. MUnit's mocking support removes that dependency entirely by intercepting specific processors and substituting a canned response.

Mocking an HTTP Request

Suppose a flow named get-customer-flow calls an HTTP Request connector to fetch customer data from an external service, then transforms the response. Instead of hitting the real endpoint, mock-when intercepts any processor matching the given criteria and substitutes a payload via then-return.

<munit:test name="get-customer-flow-returns-transformed-payload"
            description="Mocks the HTTP Request call and verifies transformation logic">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[output application/json --- { id: 42, name: 'Ada Lovelace', status: 'ACTIVE' }]"/>
        <munit-tools:attributes value="#[{statusCode: 200}]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="get-customer-flow"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.name]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('Ada Lovelace')]"/>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.status]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('ACTIVE')]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Mocking a Database Select

Database mocking follows the same shape, matching on the db:select processor and returning a canned result set as a list of maps, which is exactly what the real connector would hand back to the flow.

<munit:test name="find-orders-by-customer-returns-order-list"
            description="Mocks the Database Select and validates row-to-payload mapping">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:select">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Orders_DB_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[[
          { orderId: 1001, customerId: 42, total: 89.99 },
          { orderId: 1002, customerId: 42, total: 15.50 }
        ]]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="find-orders-by-customer-flow"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[sizeOf(payload)]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(2)]"/>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload[0].total]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(89.99)]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Matching Precisely with with-attributes

The with-attributes block is what keeps mocks from accidentally intercepting the wrong processor when a flow has more than one HTTP Request or Database connector configured. Matching on config-ref is the most reliable strategy since every connector configuration has a unique name, but you can also match on other processor attributes such as a specific query or path when a single config is reused for multiple operations.

Simulating Failures, Not Just Happy Paths

The real value of mocking shows up when testing error handling, since forcing a real downstream service to fail on demand is often impractical. then-return can be replaced with then-throw to simulate a connectivity error or timeout and verify the flow's error handler behaves correctly.

<munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
  <munit-tools:with-attributes>
    <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
  </munit-tools:with-attributes>
  <munit-tools:then-throw class="org.mule.extension.http.api.error.HttpTimeoutException"/>
</munit-tools:mock-when>

Confirming a Mock Was Actually Called

Returning a canned value only tells you what the flow does with a given input — it doesn't confirm the flow actually reached that processor, or reached it the expected number of times. verify-call closes that gap by asserting on invocation count after execution, which is especially useful for confirming that a retry policy called an HTTP Request connector three times, or that a conditional branch skipped a database write entirely under certain input conditions.

<munit:validation>
  <munit-tools:verify-call processor="http:request" times="1">
    <munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
    </munit-tools:with-attributes>
  </munit-tools:verify-call>
  <munit-tools:verify-call processor="db:select" times="0"/>
</munit:validation>

Combining a payload assertion with a verify-call check gives a much stronger guarantee than either alone: the first confirms the flow produced the right output, and the second confirms it got there by actually exercising the code path the test intends to cover, rather than short-circuiting somewhere earlier through unrelated logic.

Keeping HTTP and Database Mocks Independent

When a single flow calls both an external HTTP service and a database, it's worth mocking both in the same test rather than only one, since real flow logic often depends on combining their results — for example, enriching a database record with data fetched from an HTTP call before persisting it back. Defining both mocks in the same munit:behavior block, each scoped tightly with with-attributes, keeps the two independent so a change to one mock's canned response doesn't have unintended effects on the other's matching logic.

  • mock-when intercepts a specific processor type; with-attributes narrows the match to a specific config or operation.
  • then-return supplies a canned payload and attributes, standing in for a real HTTP response or database result set.
  • Database mocks typically return a list of maps, mirroring the real db:select connector's output shape.
  • then-throw simulates connectivity failures and timeouts to test error-handling paths without a real outage.
  • verify-call confirms a mocked processor was actually invoked (and how many times), complementing payload assertions.
  • Precise matching on config-ref prevents mocks from silently intercepting the wrong connector in flows with multiple similar operations.

subtopics.title: Assertions in MUnit
subtopics.meta_description: Explore MUnit's assert-that component and the MunitTools matcher library, including equalTo, containsString and hasSize, for validating your test results.
subtopics.summary: A guide to MUnit's assert-that component and the MunitTools matcher library for validating flow outcomes.
subtopics.content_html:
Mocking sets up the conditions for a test; assertions are what actually determine whether it passes or fails. MUnit's assertion toolkit, centered on <munit-tools:assert-that>, is built around Hamcrest-style matchers exposed through the MunitTools DataWeave module, giving you expressive, readable checks against the payload, variables, attributes, or any DataWeave expression.

assert-that

The basic pattern evaluates an expression and compares it against a matcher passed to is:

<munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.status]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('ACTIVE')]" />
<munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.customers]" is="#[MunitTools::not(MunitTools::nullValue())]" />
<munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[sizeOf(payload)]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(3)]" />

Common Matchers

MatcherChecks
equalTo(value)Exact equality with the expected value.
nullValue() / notNullValue()Whether the expression evaluates to null.
containsString(str)A string contains a given substring.
greaterThan(n) / lessThan(n)Numeric comparisons.
hasSize(n)Collection or array has exactly n elements.
everyItem(matcher)Every element of a collection satisfies the inner matcher.
not(matcher)Negates another matcher.
allOf(m1, m2, ...) / anyOf(m1, m2, ...)Combine multiple matchers with AND / OR logic.

Asserting on the Whole Event

Assertions aren't limited to the payload. You can check variables, error state, or HTTP-facing attributes set during execution:

<munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[vars.httpStatus]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(201)]" />
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[attributes.headers.'content-type']" is="#[MunitTools::containsString('application/json')]" />
</munit:validation>

assert and assert-equals

For simpler boolean or direct-equality checks, MUnit also offers lighter-weight assertion components:

<munit-tools:assert-equals actual="#[payload.total]" expected="#[100]" />
<munit-tools:assert condition="#[payload.items != []]" message="Order must contain at least one item" />

assert-that with MunitTools matchers is generally preferred for anything beyond a trivial equality check, since matcher failures produce far more descriptive messages (showing both the expected matcher description and actual value) than a plain boolean assertion.

Testing Error Assertions

When a test expects the flow to raise an error rather than complete successfully, wrap the execution block's expected failure using expectedErrorType on the test itself, or catch it and assert on the resulting payload if the flow's own error handler produces a response body:

<munit:test name="create-customer-invalid-payload-test" expectedErrorType="APP:INVALID_CUSTOMER">
    <munit:execution>
        <flow-ref name="validate-customer-subflow" />
    </munit:execution>
</munit:test>
Tip: Prefer several focused assert-that calls over one giant assertion on the entire payload object — when a focused assertion fails, the test report tells you exactly which field was wrong.

Reading Assertion Failure Messages

One of the biggest advantages of Hamcrest-style matchers is the quality of their failure output. When assert-that fails, MUnit reports both what the matcher expected and what it actually found — for example, "Expected: a string containing 'ACTIVE' but: was 'PENDING'" — which is usually enough to diagnose the problem without attaching a debugger or adding extra logging. This becomes especially valuable in CI pipelines, where a developer investigating a failed build only has the test report to go on. Writing assertions with descriptive matchers rather than opaque boolean checks is therefore not just a style preference; it materially speeds up how quickly a team can triage a broken build days or weeks after the test was originally written.

Key Points

  • assert-that combined with MunitTools matchers is the primary way to validate outcomes in MUnit.
  • Matchers cover equality, null checks, string content, numeric comparisons, and collection checks, and can be combined with allOf/anyOf/not.
  • Assertions can target payload, variables, attributes, or any DataWeave expression against the resulting event.
  • Use expectedErrorType on a test to verify a flow is expected to raise a specific error.

subtopics.title: Testing Batch Jobs and Schedulers with MUnit
subtopics.meta_description: How to test a Mule batch job's on-complete phase and a Scheduler-triggered flow in MUnit by invoking the underlying triggered logic flow directly instead.
subtopics.summary: Batch jobs and scheduled flows both run outside a normal request/response cycle, so MUnit tests them by invoking the triggered flow directly and mocking its steps.
subtopics.content_html:
Batch jobs and Scheduler-triggered flows share a common testing challenge: neither one is invoked by an inbound request, so there's no natural request/response boundary for a test to call. MUnit handles both the same way — by treating the batch job or the scheduled flow as just another flow that can be referenced directly, then mocking whatever it touches internally.

Testing a Batch Job's On-Complete Phase

A batch job typically has a Process phase that operates on individual records, and an On Complete phase that runs once after all records finish, often used to log summary statistics or send a notification. The On Complete phase receives a BatchJobResult containing counts of successful and failed records, which makes it a good candidate for isolated testing — you can construct that result directly rather than running an entire batch job through thousands of records.

<munit:test name="batch-job-on-complete-sends-summary-notification"
            description="Verifies the on-complete phase builds and sends a correct summary message">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Notification_Service_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:attributes value="#[{statusCode: 200}]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <set-variable variableName="batchJobResult"
      value="#[{ successfulRecords: 97, failedRecords: 3, totalRecords: 100 }]"/>
    <flow-ref name="customer-import-batch-on-complete"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.summary]"
      is="#[MunitTools::containsString('97 of 100')]"/>
    <munit-tools:verify-call processor="http:request" times="1">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Notification_Service_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
    </munit-tools:verify-call>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

The key technique here is extracting the On Complete logic into its own referenceable flow (rather than leaving it as an inline, unnamed phase inside the batch job definition) so MUnit can invoke it directly and feed it a synthetic batchJobResult variable, instead of running the whole batch job with real input records.

Testing a Scheduler-Triggered Flow

A flow starting with a Scheduler component runs on a timer with no inbound message to send, which means a test cannot "call" it the way it would call an HTTP-triggered flow. The practical approach is to split the flow in two: a thin flow containing only the Scheduler source, and a second, referenceable flow containing the actual logic that the Scheduler triggers via flow-ref. MUnit then tests the second flow directly, bypassing the Scheduler component entirely, since the test doesn't want to actually wait for a timer to fire.

<munit:test name="nightly-cleanup-flow-removes-expired-records"
            description="Invokes the scheduler's target logic flow directly, without waiting on the timer">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:delete">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Cleanup_DB_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[{ affectedRows: 12 }]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="nightly-cleanup-logic"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.affectedRows]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(12)]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Why Splitting Trigger From Logic Matters

Both examples rely on the same architectural habit: keeping the trigger component (Scheduler, or the batch job's phase wiring) as thin as possible, and moving the actual business logic into a separately named, referenceable flow. This isn't just a testing convenience — it also makes the logic reusable if it ever needs to be triggered a different way, such as manually via an admin endpoint in addition to the nightly schedule.

  • Batch and Scheduler flows have no natural request to send, so tests invoke the underlying logic flow directly via flow-ref.
  • Splitting trigger components (Scheduler, batch phase wiring) from business logic into separate flows is what makes direct invocation possible.
  • For batch On Complete testing, construct a synthetic batchJobResult variable rather than running a full batch with real records.
  • verify-call confirms a mocked processor was actually invoked the expected number of times, not just that the flow didn't error.
  • This pattern keeps tests fast and deterministic by avoiding real timers and large record sets entirely.

subtopics.title: MUnit Test Coverage
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how MUnit measures application and resource test coverage, and how to enforce minimum coverage thresholds using the munit-maven-plugin in CI/CD.
subtopics.summary: How MUnit coverage reporting works in Studio and Maven, and how to enforce minimum coverage thresholds in CI/CD.
subtopics.content_html:
Writing tests is only half the story — knowing how much of your application they actually exercise is what turns testing from a checkbox into a meaningful quality gate. MUnit's test coverage reporting measures what percentage of your Mule flows and resources are touched during a test run, both in Anypoint Studio and as part of a Maven build.

Running Coverage in Studio

When you run an MUnit suite in Anypoint Studio via Run As > MUnit Test with Coverage, Studio highlights each processor in your flows to show whether it was executed by at least one test, giving an immediate visual signal of untested branches — for example, an on-error-continue block that no test ever triggers.

Enforcing Coverage With the Maven Plugin

For CI/CD pipelines, the munit-maven-plugin can enforce minimum coverage thresholds and fail the build if they aren't met:

# pom.xml excerpt
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.mulesoft.munit.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>munit-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <configuration>
    <coverage>
      <runCoverage>true</runCoverage>
      <failBuild>true</failBuild>
      <requiredApplicationCoverage>80</requiredApplicationCoverage>
      <requiredResourceCoverage>70</requiredResourceCoverage>
      <formats>
        <format>html</format>
        <format>json</format>
      </formats>
      <ignoreFiles>
        <ignoreFile>**/generated-error-flows.xml</ignoreFile>
      </ignoreFiles>
    </coverage>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

Coverage Metrics Explained

  • Application coverage — the percentage of processors, across all flows in the application, that were exercised by at least one test.
  • Resource coverage — the percentage of individual flow files (or resources) that have at least some associated test coverage, useful for spotting entire files with zero tests.
  • requiredApplicationCoverage / requiredResourceCoverage — thresholds that, when unmet, fail the build if failBuild is true, making coverage an enforced quality gate rather than a suggestion.

Reading Coverage Reports

The plugin can emit HTML reports (for humans browsing coverage locally or in a CI artifact) and JSON reports (for feeding into dashboards or quality tools). The HTML report typically breaks coverage down file by file, so you can quickly identify which flows have the weakest test coverage and prioritize writing tests there first.

What High Coverage Does and Doesn't Guarantee

A high coverage percentage confirms that a processor executed during testing, but it says nothing about whether the assertions around it were meaningful. It is entirely possible to reach 100% coverage with tests that never assert anything beyond "the flow didn't throw." Coverage should be treated as a floor that flags untested code paths, not a substitute for reviewing whether assertions actually validate correct business behavior.

Tip: Use ignoreFiles to exclude auto-generated APIkit routing flows from coverage requirements, since their logic is simple dispatch code already implicitly exercised whenever any resource/method flow is tested.

Key Points

  • MUnit coverage reports show which processors and flow files were exercised by the test suite.
  • The munit-maven-plugin can enforce minimum application and resource coverage thresholds in CI/CD.
  • HTML and JSON report formats support both human review and automated dashboards.
  • High coverage alone doesn't guarantee good tests; pair it with meaningful, specific assertions.

subtopics.title: MUnit Best Practices and CI/CD Integration
subtopics.meta_description: Practical MUnit best practices and how to run munit:test with enforced coverage thresholds via the Mule Maven plugin inside a CI/CD pipeline reliably.
subtopics.summary: Running MUnit as an enforced, coverage-gated step in the Maven build turns tests from an optional habit into a build-breaking safety net.
subtopics.content_html:
Writing MUnit tests is only half the story — the other half is making sure they actually run on every change, and that a drop in coverage or a broken test fails the build loudly rather than getting merged quietly. This comes down to a handful of practices in how flows are structured, plus a small amount of Maven and pipeline configuration.

Design Flows to Be Testable

Flows that mix a trigger (HTTP Listener, Scheduler, batch phase) directly with business logic in the same flow are harder to test in isolation, because the trigger component itself can't be easily invoked from a test. Extracting the logic into its own named, referenceable flow — called via flow-ref from the trigger flow — means the test suite can invoke that logic flow directly, without needing to simulate an HTTP request or wait on a timer. This single habit is responsible for most of the difference between a codebase that's pleasant to test and one where every test needs elaborate workarounds.

Avoid Hardcoded Test Data

Hardcoded values scattered across dozens of test files make it hard to tell which value a given assertion actually depends on, and they make updating a shared test fixture painful. Centralizing common test payloads and mock responses in reusable DataWeave files under src/test/resources, referenced from multiple tests, keeps fixtures consistent and makes it obvious when a change to expected data is intentional versus accidental.

<munit-tools:then-return>
  <munit-tools:payload value="#[readUrl('classpath://testdata/customer-response.json', 'application/json')]"/>
</munit-tools:then-return>

Running MUnit via the Mule Maven Plugin

The munit-maven-plugin, driven through the Mule Maven Plugin, runs the full MUnit suite as part of the Maven build lifecycle, meaning mvn test (or mvn verify) executes every MUnit test in the project the same way a CI pipeline would, with no separate tooling required.

<plugin>
  <groupId>com.mulesoft.munit.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>munit-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>test</id>
      <phase>test</phase>
      <goals>
        <goal>test</goal>
        <goal>coverage-report</goal>
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
  <configuration>
    <coverage>
      <runCoverage>true</runCoverage>
      <failBuild>true</failBuild>
      <requiredApplicationCoverage>80</requiredApplicationCoverage>
      <requiredResourceCoverage>70</requiredResourceCoverage>
    </coverage>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

With failBuild set to true, if application coverage drops below the configured threshold — say a new flow was added with no corresponding test — the Maven build fails, which in turn fails the pipeline. This is what turns coverage from an informational metric into an enforced gate.

Wiring It Into a CI/CD Pipeline

Because the tests run through a standard Maven phase, most CI/CD tools need nothing more than an ordinary build step.

mvn clean test \
  -Dmule.env=test \
  -DfailIfNoTests=false

Running this on every pull request, before merge, ensures a broken test or an insufficiently tested new flow is caught before it reaches a shared branch, rather than being discovered later during a deployment. Publishing the generated coverage report (typically Cobertura or a similar format) as a pipeline artifact also gives reviewers a quick way to see exactly which lines are untested, rather than trusting a single pass/fail percentage.

Other Practical Tips

  • Group related tests into suite files by feature area (e.g., orders-tests.xml, customers-tests.xml) rather than one enormous test file, so failures are easy to locate.
  • Use munit:before-test and munit:after-test blocks for setup/teardown shared across a suite instead of repeating it in every test.
  • Keep mock configuration close to the specific test that needs it rather than global, to avoid one test's mock silently affecting another.
  • Extracting business logic into referenceable flows, separate from triggers, is the single biggest enabler of testability.
  • Centralized test fixtures in src/test/resources reduce duplication and make intentional data changes easier to spot.
  • The munit-maven-plugin's coverage-report goal, combined with failBuild and threshold settings, turns coverage into a build gate.
  • Running mvn test in CI on every pull request catches undertested or broken flows before merge.
  • Publishing coverage reports as pipeline artifacts helps reviewers see exactly what's untested, not just a percentage.
